content: People often have to rely on multiple data systems to gather even basic information about the incidence and prevalence of violence against women (VAW). This reliance can be problematic because these data sources are typically designed for purposes other than monitoring the scope of VAW. For instance, police collect data on violence against women primarily to apprehend and prosecute perpetrators, which may result in limited documentation about the victims. Similarly, hospitals focus on providing optimal patient care and billing, which means they may not record details about the perpetrator or even recognize the violence as such. Until routine identification and documentation of VAW become part of standard patient care, hospital records will remain of limited value for public health surveillance of VAW. These limitations suggest that data from multiple systems are likely needed to produce more accurate estimates of the number of women affected by violence. The task of obtaining surveillance data is further complicated by the repetitive nature of certain types of VAW, such as intimate partner violence (IPV). This makes it difficult to determine whether the data reflect the number of individuals affected or the number of violent incidents. Police may document each assault separately, even if all incidents involve the same perpetrator, while hospitals may record repeated incidents in a single patient file. In addition to these logistical challenges, social barriers also hinder the collection of accurate VAW data. These barriers include the taboo nature of the topic, feelings of guilt and shame that prevent victims and perpetrators from self-identifying, and a lack of training or fear of repercussions that discourage agency personnel from recording VAW cases in official records. Furthermore, only a small fraction of VAW victims seek help from either the criminal justice or healthcare systems. Recognizing the need to improve the quality of available data on VAW, the National Center for Injury Prevention and Control (NCIPC) at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) initiated efforts to address some of the conceptual and logistical challenges inherent in this task. To make the task more manageable, the CDC decided to focus on developing data elements for surveillance of one subset of VAW: intimate partner violence. Available data suggest that VAW is a significant public health problem in the United States. For example, police data indicate that 3,631 women were murdered in 1996, with 30% of these homicides committed by a spouse or ex-spouse. Additionally, 3 million women are physically assaulted annually, and approximately 200,000 women are raped annually by a current or former intimate partner. Eight million women have been raped by a current or former intimate partner. Although these statistics highlight the magnitude of the problem, some believe that VAW statistics underrepresent the issue, while others argue that reports of VAW are exaggerated. Much of the debate about the number of women affected by violence is clouded by a lack of consensus on the definition of violence against women. The term has been used to describe a wide range of acts, including murder, rape, sexual assault, physical assault, emotional abuse, battering, stalking, prostitution, genital mutilation, sexual harassment, and pornography. Researchers have used these terms inconsistently, leading to varied conclusions about the incidence and prevalence of VAW. The lack of consistent information about the number of women affected by violence limits our ability to respond to the problem in several ways. It hinders our ability to gauge the magnitude of VAW relative to other public health issues, identify high-risk groups who might benefit from targeted interventions, and monitor changes in the incidence and prevalence of VAW over time. This, in turn, limits our ability to evaluate the effectiveness of prevention and intervention efforts. Higher-quality and more timely estimates of VAW incidence and prevalence could benefit a wide audience, including policymakers, researchers, public health practitioners, victim advocates, service providers, and media professionals. However, obtaining accurate and reliable estimates is complicated by several factors. There are no established, ongoing surveillance activities for VAW. To address this, the CDC funded state health departments in Massachusetts, Michigan, and Rhode Island to pilot methods for statewide IPV surveillance among women. These efforts involved an extensive review of the literature, the development of draft definitions and data elements, and consultations with experts in VAW and data collection. The process included multiple meetings and revisions to refine the definitions and data elements. The recommended data elements for IPV surveillance include four types of violence: physical violence, sexual violence, threats of physical or sexual violence, and psychological/emotional abuse. However, one violent episode may involve all four types of violence. A limitation of the current system is that it can count episodes involving specific types of violence but cannot provide a total count of discrete violent episodes or information about the co-occurrence of different types of violence within all episodes. The IPV surveillance system will allow for the collection of information about the co-occurrence of different types of violence for the most recent violent episode perpetrated by any intimate partner. The definitions and data elements were developed to enable data collection for both female and male IPV victims, although initial pilot tests focus on IPV against women. Ethical and safety considerations are paramount in all research on VAW. No data should be collected or stored in a way that jeopardizes a woman's safety. Confidentiality must be preserved, and data linkage across multiple sources should be achieved through mechanisms such as encryption of unique identifiers. The recommended data elements currently include 50 items, but this list may be shortened based on feedback from pilot projects and other locations. Desirable data elements that are not feasible to collect as part of a surveillance system will need to be collected through other means. No single agency is likely to collect all the recommended data elements. Instead, data from multiple sources, such as healthcare and police records, should be integrated using a relational database. A unique identifier will be needed to link data across all sources. The ultimate goal of IPV surveillance is to estimate the number of people affected by IPV, describe their characteristics, and document the number and types of IPV episodes, associated injuries, and other consequences. Counting injuries is a common proxy for estimating the number of people affected, but the repetitive nature of IPV and the co-occurrence of multiple forms of violence may reduce the accuracy of this approach. To obtain more accurate estimates, mechanisms for linking data within and across different sources using unique identifiers will need to be developed. The recommended data elements include four discrete types of violence: physical violence, sexual violence, threats of physical or sexual violence, and psychological/emotional abuse. However, one violent episode may involve all four types of violence. The IPV surveillance system will allow for the collection of information about the co-occurrence of different types of violence for the most recent violent episode perpetrated by any intimate partner. Each data element is numbered for ease of reference and includes a code set specifying recommended coding values and instructions for handling cases where the data element is not applicable. The accuracy and completeness of IPV data depend on the documentation provided by the agency supplying the information. The CDC has funded pilot tests of these data elements in Massachusetts, Michigan, and Rhode Island to assess the feasibility and utility of collecting this information on IPV victims. Other jurisdictions are encouraged to conduct limited pilot tests as well. After these tests are completed, the definitions and data elements will be refined to make data collection more feasible as part of an IPV surveillance system. Eventually, the goal is to develop data elements and definitions for the surveillance of other forms of family violence, such as child abuse and elder abuse, and other forms of violence against women.
